newsitem.title: GERMANY: German bourse says firms must sign merger code.
newsitem.headline: German bourse says firms must sign merger code.

text.p: Germany's bourse, Deutsche Boerse AG, said on Tuesday that from January 1998 only companies who accepted its takeover code would be allowed inclusion on its DAX and MDAX share indices.

While the bourse has made veiled threats to this effect before, a statement on Tuesday afternoon explicitly stated that the bourse management board would strike companies off the indices who refuse to agree to abide by the voluntary code.

The bourse also said that companies which refuse to recognise the takeover code would be listed as such on a host of different platforms, such as sector lists, index brochures, statistics or Internet sites.
The German DAX-100 index is made up of the blue-chip DAX index of Germany's 30 largest listed companies, and the M-DAX index of 70 medium-sized firms.
Germany introduced the voluntary takeover code in October 1995, calling on companies to pledge to stand by its rules and insisting that the code helps smaller shareholders.
But the code has so far found the support of only 270 firms out of a total of 683 listed companies. Of the top 100 firms in the DAX-100 index, only 61 have agreed to abide by the takeover code.

Some firms have agreed to the rules, but then withdrawn their support. The industrial group Metallgesellschaft removed its support for the code after it was relegated against its will from the DAX index to the MDAX.

Under the terms of the agreement, a company which owns a stake of more than 50 percent in a target company is required to make an offer to outstanding shareholders, except in instances where an exemption has been granted.
The company has 18 months to make an offer to outstanding shareholders, although the rules indicate that the price should be near to market levels at the time the offer is made.
Exemptions could be made when the firm is an approved majority shareholder and is accepted as such by the target company's annual shareholder meeting.

The code in many ways resembles Britain's well-established takeover and mergers agreement, whcih is also not legally binding. But the British version calls for an offer at an earlier level, once a stake reaches 30 percent.
Germany hopes its action on takeovers will prevent Brussels from drawing up European merger laws, which could be tougher than the existing voluntary code.
The existing rules are aimed at creating greater transparency in the famously incestous network of German industrial cross-holdings, which has been nicknamed "Fortress Germany" by foreign predators.
